title: Peter Pan
author: J. M. Barrie
short_summary: Peter Pan, a boy who will not grow up, flies into the Darling children's nursery one night looking for his lost shadow, and carries Wendy, John and Michael away to Neverland. There they find the Lost Boys, Tinker Bell, mermaids, Tiger Lily and Captain Hook — who has hated Peter ever since Peter fed his hand to a crocodile. Wendy becomes a mother to them all, and eventually has to decide whether to stay a child for ever.
extended_summary:
Peter comes back to the Darlings' nursery for the shadow he left behind, and Wendy sews it on for him. In return he teaches the three children to fly and takes them to Neverland — second to the right, and then straight on till morning.

Tinker Bell, who is jealous, tells the Lost Boys that Wendy is a bird Peter wants shot, and Tootles fires an arrow at her the moment she arrives. Wendy survives, the boys build a little house around where she has fallen, and she becomes the mother of the household underground. Above them the island runs on its own rules: mermaids in the lagoon, Tiger Lily and her people, and Captain Hook and the pirates of the Jolly Roger.

Hook has one arm, because Peter threw the other to a crocodile — which has followed him ever since, and which Hook can hear coming because it also swallowed a clock. When Hook poisons Peter's medicine, Tinker Bell drinks it instead, and is only saved because children everywhere are asked to clap if they believe in fairies. The children are captured, Hook is defeated, and Wendy takes everyone home.

Wendy grows up. Peter comes back for her daughter Jane, and later for Jane's daughter Margaret — every spring-cleaning time, except when he forgets — and Barrie says it will go on like that for as long as there are children.

questions.prompt: Why does Peter come to the Darlings' nursery in the first place?

options: He has left his shadow behind and wants it back
He has heard that Wendy tells very good stories
He is looking for a mother for the Lost Boys
He is hiding from Captain Hook and the pirates

questions.explanation: Everything else follows from an errand: he comes back for a shadow, Wendy wakes up and sews it on, and the flying lessons and Neverland are only what happens next. Barrie starts the biggest story in children's literature with a mislaid piece of laundry.

questions.prompt: Asked the way to Neverland, Peter gives the famous directions: "Second to the right, and then straight on till ___."
questions.explanation: It is not a route, it is a rhythm — as Barrie later admits, Peter made it up on the spot and the children only reached the island because they were following him rather than the directions. The line is the most quoted sentence in the book.

questions.prompt: What happens to Wendy the moment she first arrives over Neverland?

options: Tootles shoots her with an arrow
The mermaids pull her into the lagoon
Hook's pirates capture her at once
She loses her shadow among the trees

questions.explanation: Tinker Bell, jealous, tells the Lost Boys that Wendy is a bird Peter wants shot, and Tootles does it immediately to please him. It is a shocking scene for a children's book — she is saved only by the acorn button she is wearing — and Tootles never quite recovers from it.

questions.prompt: Why can Captain Hook always hear the crocodile coming?

options: It swallowed a clock, which is still ticking
It sings to itself as it swims up the creek
Smee rings a bell whenever he sees it
The birds on the island always cry a warning

questions.explanation: Peter threw Hook's arm to the crocodile, and it has followed him ever since, hoping for the rest. The clock is Barrie's real joke: Hook is not frightened of a reptile, he is frightened of time — audibly, all day, getting closer.

questions.prompt: Put the events of the story in the order they happen.

items: Peter comes back for the shadow he left behind
Wendy sews the shadow onto his feet
The three children are taught to fly to Neverland
Tootles shoots Wendy with an arrow as she arrives
The Lost Boys build a little house around her
Tinker Bell drinks the poison meant for Peter

questions.explanation: The first three steps take one evening, and the whole plot of the book is set in motion before anyone reaches the island. Notice also that Wendy is nearly killed on the day she arrives — Neverland is not a safe place, and Barrie makes that clear immediately.

questions.prompt: Match each character to their part in the story.

right: The dog who is the children's nurse
The jealous fairy who drinks the poison
The Lost Boy who fires the arrow
The boatswain who serves Captain Hook

questions.explanation: Barrie's minor characters do all the real damage and all the real saving: a dog is the only sensible adult in the Darling house, and a fairy who tried to have Wendy killed is the one who dies for Peter a hundred pages later.

questions.prompt: Sort each detail by which world it belongs to.

options.label: A dog employed to look after the children
A shadow rolled up and put in a drawer
A window left open for a child to come back
A house built around a girl where she fell
A pirate ship anchored off the island
A crocodile with a clock inside it

questions.explanation: The nursery is already half enchanted before Peter arrives — a dog for a nurse, a shadow in a drawer, a window nobody will close. That is why the children go so easily: Barrie does not make them cross a border, he simply widens one they are already standing on.

questions.prompt: Tinker Bell drinks the poison Hook meant for Peter, and begins to die. What saves her?

options: Children clapping to show that they believe in fairies
Peter carrying her up to the mermaids' lagoon
The Lost Boys finding the antidote in Hook's cabin
Wendy giving her the acorn button from her chain

questions.explanation: Peter turns and shouts to children everywhere to clap if they believe. It is the moment the book stops pretending the reader is not there — and the reason is set up early on, when Barrie explains that a fairy dies every time a child says they do not believe.

questions.prompt: Peter Pan refuses to grow up, and offers Wendy the chance to stay in Neverland with him for ever. She goes home instead. Do you think she made the right choice? Give your reasons.
questions.explanation: Both answers can earn full marks. A strong 'right choice' answer notices that Peter forgets people, that Wendy wanted her own mother, and that the Lost Boys go home too and are glad of it. A strong 'she should have stayed' answer notices what she gives up and that Barrie clearly finds growing up a loss. The best answers notice that the book itself does not sound certain.

questions.prompt: Neverland is different for every child who dreams it — one has a lagoon, another a cave, another a wolf. Describe your own Neverland: name two things that would be in it, and one thing in it that would be dangerous.
questions.explanation: There is no single right answer. A strong answer includes the danger, because that is the point Barrie makes repeatedly: an island with nothing frightening in it would be no fun and no child dreams one. An answer that is entirely pleasant has missed how Neverland works.

questions.prompt: Captain Hook lost a hand to the crocodile because Peter threw it there. The pirate who attends him and calms him down is called ___.
questions.explanation: Smee is the only pirate anyone likes, which unsettles Hook more than anything else in the book — he cannot understand why children are not frightened of him. Barrie gives his villain a proper inner life and then lets a boy who cannot remember anything defeat him.

questions.prompt: How does the book end, years after Wendy has gone home?

options: Peter comes back for Wendy's daughter, and later her granddaughter
Peter grows up at last and settles in London near the Darlings
Wendy returns to Neverland and stays there with the Lost Boys
The window of the nursery is shut and Peter never comes again

questions.explanation: Wendy grows up; Jane goes in her place, and then Margaret goes in Jane's, and Barrie says it will go on as long as there are children. Peter has not changed at all, and he does not remember that anything has — which is presented, in the last pages, as the saddest thing in the book rather than the happiest.
